distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: first-layer clinical disease leaf for acute immune-mediated solid-organ allograft rejection, without splitting by graft organ, T-cell-mediated rejection, antibody-mediated rejection, mixed rejection, early, late, Banff grade, or severity phenotype
distillation_scope.subtype_policy: Kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas, cellular, antibody-mediated, mixed, sensitization, and immunosuppression contexts are represented as mechanisms, context axes, risk factors, treatment modifiers, and organ-specific response axes, not as disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use transplant context, time from transplant, recent immunosuppression underexposure or reduction when known, fever or systemic illness when present, and organ-specific allograft dysfunction. Biopsy Banff/pathology, C4d, donor-specific antibody, molecular rejection score, donor-derived cell-free DNA, final adjudication, treatment response, and outcome should be confirmatory or non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Recipient T cells recognize donor alloantigens and drive interstitial, endothelial, ductal, bronchial, or myocardial inflammatory injury depending on graft organ.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Donor-specific antibody and complement endothelial injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Donor-specific or non-HLA antibodies injure graft microvasculature through endothelial activation, complement deposition, C4d-positive or C4d-negative AMR, thrombosis, edema, and ischemic parenchymal stress.
Endothelialitis, capillaritis, venulitis, tissue edema, and microvascular congestion reduce perfusion and create swelling, tenderness, congestion, or impaired organ function.
Tubular, hepatocellular, biliary epithelial, cardiomyocyte, or airway/alveolar injury causes organ-specific laboratory and physiologic dysfunction.
Acute rejection may produce fever, malaise, inflammatory markers, vasoplegia, or stress physiology, but fever and leukocytosis can be absent under immunosuppression.
Renal allograft rejection causes rising creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria, oliguria, allograft tenderness, or dialysis need, with biopsy defining the rejection phenotype.

Liver allograft rejection causes aminotransferase, cholestatic, synthetic, vascular-flow, encephalopathy, lactate, and acute liver failure phenotypes depending on severity and AMR versus cellular balance.
Cardiac allograft rejection causes systolic or diastolic dysfunction, low output, congestion, arrhythmia, troponin or natriuretic peptide elevation, and cardiogenic shock.
Lung allograft rejection can cause dyspnea, cough, falling FEV1, hypoxemia, new infiltrates, pleural effusion, or respiratory failure after infection and other mimics are considered.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Severe graft failure and multiorgan decompensation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Uncontrolled rejection can progress to irreversible graft failure, shock, dialysis, respiratory failure, retransplant need, and death.

axes.shape_free_text: Patient has a transplanted solid-organ allograft that can be rejected.
Kidney allograft is the relevant graft context.
Liver allograft is the relevant graft context.
Heart allograft is the relevant graft context.
Lung allograft is the relevant graft context.
Elapsed days from transplant to the acute allograft dysfunction presentation; acute rejection can occur early or late.
Intensity of maintenance or recent transplant immunosuppression exposure.
Medication nonadherence, low trough, interrupted therapy, or deliberate reduction that increases alloimmune activity.
Recent reduction or withholding of immunosuppression for infection, malignancy, toxicity, pregnancy, or procedural reasons.
Any new graft dysfunction unexplained by baseline chronic disease, infection, vascular obstruction, ischemia, or drug toxicity.
Tenderness over a graft, most often kidney; can be absent in many rejection episodes.
Fever history during acute rejection; common in severe inflammatory or liver rejection but absent in many kidney and heart episodes.
Measured temperature; may be normal despite acute rejection under immunosuppression.
Tachycardia from fever, shock, heart allograft dysfunction, anemia, or stress physiology.
Tachypnea from pulmonary edema, respiratory allograft dysfunction, shock, acidosis, or systemic illness.
Systolic blood pressure; severe cardiac or liver rejection can present with low pressure or shock.
Mean arterial pressure; low values indicate shock or low-output state.
Persistent hypotension or shock physiology from severe graft dysfunction, vasoplegia, or low output.
Inflammatory marker that may rise in rejection but is nonspecific and often infection-confounded.
New kidney allograft dysfunction with rising creatinine, proteinuria, hematuria, oliguria, or tenderness.
Creatinine rises in kidney allograft rejection and can also rise from severe heart or liver allograft failure with hypoperfusion.
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio; can rise in kidney allograft rejection, glomerular injury, or chronic allograft disease.
Proteinuria as kidney allograft injury evidence.
Hematuria can occur with kidney allograft inflammation but is not required and overlaps infection or glomerulonephritis.
Reduced urine output from severe renal graft dysfunction or low-output multiorgan failure.
Hazard for clinically significant AKI from renal allograft rejection or severe graft-failure shock physiology.
Dialysis or renal replacement need from severe renal dysfunction, acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload.
New liver allograft dysfunction with hepatocellular, cholestatic, synthetic, vascular, encephalopathic, or ALF phenotype.
AST elevation from liver allograft hepatocellular injury; severe AMR/ischemic graft injury can cause high values.
ALT elevation from liver allograft hepatocellular injury.
Cholestatic enzyme response from bile duct injury or biliary/vascular complications.
Total bilirubin elevation from cholestatic or severe hepatocellular liver allograft dysfunction.
INR rises when liver allograft synthetic failure develops.
Hepatic encephalopathy grade during liver allograft failure.
Lactate elevation or acidosis from severe liver graft failure, cardiogenic shock, or multiorgan hypoperfusion.
Hazard for acute liver failure from severe liver allograft rejection.
New heart allograft dysfunction with systolic failure, low output, congestion, arrhythmia, or shock.
Dyspnea from heart or lung allograft dysfunction, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure.
Fatigue or malaise from systemic inflammation, heart failure, renal failure, or liver dysfunction.
Cough may accompany lung allograft rejection or pulmonary congestion in heart allograft failure.
Abdominal pain can reflect hepatic congestion, liver graft dysfunction, gut edema, or nonspecific systemic illness.
Peripheral edema from heart allograft failure, renal dysfunction, or liver dysfunction.
Elevated jugular venous pressure from heart allograft failure or volume overload.
Bibasilar crackles from pulmonary edema, congestion, infection, or lung allograft dysfunction.
Pulmonary vascular congestion or edema from heart allograft dysfunction or severe volume overload.
Cardiomegaly or enlarged cardiac silhouette in heart allograft dysfunction.
BNP rises with heart allograft dysfunction, congestion, and wall stress.
LVEF can drop acutely in cardiac allograft rejection with graft dysfunction.
Cardiac index falls in severe heart allograft dysfunction and cardiogenic shock.
Cardiac output falls during severe heart allograft dysfunction.
PCWP rises with left-sided allograft failure and congestion.
Right atrial pressure rises with right-sided or biventricular allograft dysfunction and congestion.
Bicarbonate falls with shock-related metabolic acidosis, renal failure, or severe liver failure.
Low voltage ECG can accompany cardiac allograft dysfunction, edema, effusion, or severe illness.
Hazard for cardiogenic shock from cardiac allograft rejection.
Hazard for atrial or ventricular arrhythmia during cardiac allograft rejection.
New lung allograft dysfunction with dyspnea, cough, falling FEV1, hypoxemia, infiltrates, or respiratory failure.
FEV1 percent predicted can drop in lung allograft rejection.
Oxygen saturation can fall in lung allograft rejection, pulmonary edema, or shock.
New infiltrates may appear in lung allograft rejection but also overlap infection and edema.
Hazard for oxygen or ventilatory failure from lung rejection or pulmonary edema during severe heart rejection.
DSA or compatible antibody evidence for AMR; confirmatory/post-workup unless explicitly testing that mode.
Donor-derived cell-free DNA fraction rises with allograft injury and rejection but is not presentation-only evidence unless specifically available in the test mode.
Biopsy evidence of acute rejection by organ-specific pathology criteria; confirmatory/post-workup.
Microvascular inflammation, endothelialitis, capillaritis, or venulitis on allograft biopsy; confirmatory/post-workup.
C4d deposition in graft capillaries or portal microvasculature supporting AMR; confirmatory/post-workup.
Hazard for irreversible allograft failure or loss.
Need to evaluate urgent retransplantation or graft replacement when rejection causes irreversible graft failure.
Disease-specific lifespan mortality hazard from acute transplant rejection through shock, organ failure, graft loss, infection/treatment complications, and unavailable salvage.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Allograft dysfunction is meaningful only when a transplanted graft exists.
Underexposure raises alloimmune activation, but rejection can occur despite therapeutic levels.
AMR often couples DSA with microvascular inflammation, though C4d-negative and DSA-negative patterns exist.
Rising creatinine is a major kidney allograft dysfunction signal.
Marked creatinine rise represents AKI hazard in graft or multiorgan failure.
AST and ALT rise together from hepatocellular allograft injury.
INR elevation marks loss of liver synthetic reserve.
Encephalopathy is an acute liver failure defining event when synthetic dysfunction is present.
Severe LVEF reduction in heart allograft rejection drives shock risk.
Low measured cardiac index is direct low-output physiology.
Elevated filling pressure causes pulmonary congestion and dyspnea.
Low-output or distributive shock can cause renal hypoperfusion and dialysis need.
Irreversible graft loss raises mortality risk, especially for heart, liver, lung, and unavailable retransplant contexts.
Acute liver failure from rejection can be rapidly fatal without rescue or retransplantation.
Cardiogenic shock in cardiac allograft rejection is a major acute mortality pathway.
Respiratory failure from lung allograft rejection or pulmonary edema raises mortality hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Escalating immunosuppression can worsen uncontrolled infection; transplant teams balance both risks.
Calcineurin inhibitor exposure may need adjustment when nephrotoxicity or renal dysfunction is present.
Steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection and may blur mimic evaluation.
Steroids worsen hyperglycemia and infection susceptibility.
Severe baseline lymphopenia raises infectious toxicity.
T-cell depletion can worsen CMV and other opportunistic infections.

toxicity_axis_effects.interpretation: Lymphocyte depletion raises CMV, fungal, viral, and bacterial infection risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: AMR benefit depends on antibody-mediated biology.
Severe shock requires parallel organ support during antibody removal.
Anti-CD20 therapy requires viral reactivation risk management.
B-cell depletion can worsen humoral immune deficiency.
Proteasome inhibitors are most biologically aligned with plasma-cell-rich or antibody-refractory patterns.
Bortezomib can worsen neuropathy.
Complement-mediated microvascular injury is the intended target.
Terminal complement blockade increases meningococcal and encapsulated bacterial risk.
Shock physiology determines need for pressors, inotropes, and monitoring.
ALF needs ICU, coagulation, glucose, ammonia, airway, and transplant rescue planning.
Persistent shock despite inotropes is the context where MCS changes survival trajectory.
Cannulation and anticoagulation increase bleeding risk.

toxicity_axis_effects.interpretation: Temporary MCS requires vascular access and anticoagulation.

treatments.treatment_name: Renal replacement therapy for rejection complications

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RRT benefit requires renal or metabolic indication.

treatments.treatment_name: Urgent retransplant or graft replacement evaluation

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Replacement is relevant only when graft failure is severe and salvage is insufficient.
Uncontrolled infection can prevent or delay retransplant.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Acute rejection requires a graft and may occur early after transplantation, after immunosuppression changes, or late with chronic sensitization/nonadherence.
Kidney allograft rejection expresses primarily as creatinine rise, proteinuria, hematuria, oliguria, tenderness, or dialysis need.
Liver allograft rejection expresses as hepatocellular, cholestatic, synthetic, encephalopathic, and severe ALF phenotypes.
Heart allograft rejection expresses as systolic dysfunction, congestion, arrhythmia, low cardiac index, and cardiogenic shock.
Lung allograft rejection expresses as dyspnea, cough, falling FEV1, hypoxemia, infiltrates, or respiratory failure.
Missed medications, low troughs, malabsorption, drug interactions, or intentional reduction increase T-cell and antibody-mediated rejection risk.
Prior transplant, pregnancy, transfusion, high HLA mismatch, positive crossmatch, or de novo DSA shifts phenotype toward AMR, microvascular inflammation, complement injury, and graft loss.
Immunosuppression reduction can trigger rejection, while escalation can worsen infection, viral replication, malignancy, cytopenia, or drug toxicity.
Prior rejection, chronic graft dysfunction, donor-specific antibodies, or chronic allograft vasculopathy/nephropathy reduces reserve and raises graft-loss hazard during acute rejection.
Heart, liver, and lung graft failure generally has higher immediate mortality than isolated kidney graft failure unless retransplantation, mechanical support, dialysis, or other rescue is feasible.

supportive_care: Coordinate early with the transplant organ team; acute rejection is a graft-context disease and treatment must balance rejection control against infection, drug toxicity, and graft reserve.

Preserve presentation evidence separately from post-workup confirmation: biopsy Banff/pathology, C4d, DSA, molecular diagnostics, dd-cfDNA, and final adjudication should not be consumed in presentation-only ranking.

Exclude and concurrently treat urgent mimics or co-drivers when clinically present: infection, vascular thrombosis or stenosis, ischemia-reperfusion injury, drug toxicity, recurrent primary disease, biliary/urinary obstruction, cardiac allograft vasculopathy, pulmonary edema, and chronic allograft dysfunction.

Use organ-specific monitoring: creatinine, urine protein and urine output for kidney; AST/ALT, bilirubin, INR, lactate, glucose, ammonia, encephalopathy, and Doppler/vascular assessment for liver; BNP/troponin, ECG, echo, hemodynamics, and rhythm monitoring for heart; spirometry, oxygenation, chest imaging, and bronchoscopy/infection evaluation for lung.

Provide ICU-level support when severe graft failure emerges: vasopressors/inotropes, mechanical circulatory support, ventilatory support, renal replacement therapy, coagulopathy/metabolic management, and retransplant evaluation when appropriate.

Monitor treatment toxicity: opportunistic infection, CMV/BK/EBV reactivation, cytopenias, hyperglycemia, nephrotoxicity, serum sickness, infusion reactions, hypogammaglobulinemia, neuropathy, complement-blockade infection risk, and bleeding or vascular complications from apheresis/MCS.
quality_notes: The disease prompt scope is pure disease name: Acute transplant rejection. Graft organ and rejection mechanism are not disease-name qualifiers.
DSA, C4d, Banff/pathology, biopsy, molecular score, and dd-cfDNA axes are included for post-workup structure but should remain non-ranking in presentation-only case JSON.
